The project week consists of 9 days of preparation across the span of several weeks in March 2027, 1 day of putting on the pop-up exhibition, and 1 day of summarizing and reflecting on the experience. The dates of the course (where students are expected to be present between 9.30 and 16.30) are: 1.3., 2.3., 3.3., 8.3., 9.3., 10.3., 15.3., 16.3., 17.3., 20.3. (exhibition day), and 31.3.
objective: At the end of the module, students will have designed and implemented a mobile exhibition on the topic of trust. They will have gained practical experience in project management and teamwork, honed their skills in planning and executing an event, and applied their creativity, leadership and problem-solving abilities. As the aim of the module is to put together a science outreach event, students will have learned how to engage and connect with the local community and communicate research findings in an accessible way, by which they will also have gained experience in public speaking and presentation.
prerequisites:
English language fluency
To register, interested students should send an e-mail to laura.schlingloff-nemecz@tum.de, briefly describing their background and why they are interested in the topic of the course (2-3 sentences).
title: Project week: Communicating Curiosity – A Science Outreach Pop-Up Exhibition

name: Project Weeks: Data Design Studio for AI-Powered EdTech
content: Would you like to become an educational technology researcher? Are you interested in educational technology design? Are you dreaming of building educational technology? To get started, you will need knowledge about how data flows in and out of educational technology and may influence and capture human behavior and learning. Integrating data-oriented thinking is not trivial. "Data Design Studio” will provide a dive into the world of data-driven thinking. This Project Weeks course is an intensive, student-centered, and project-oriented learning experience of a scaffolded process for data collection design in the context of AI-powered EdTech. This project-based course targets all TUM students interested in AI-powered EdTech at any level (Bachelor, Master, PhD) and any school. Participating students will have the opportunity to select a real educational problem and to design and implement data flows for AI-powered EdTech that could tackle this problem. Participants will work independently with special instructional materials and instructor feedback to support their learning process at different stages of their projects.
objective: By engaging with specific learning cases that describe real-world educational problems, participants in this course will investigate how educational tools align with learning theories that describe the intended effects of technology on learners. By engaging with a selection of data collection tools (e.g., video, sensors, audio), participants will familiarize themselves with primary data sources and their limitations for generating knowledge about teaching and learning. The participants will engage in the process of designing and critiquing data flows for educational technologies through a hands-on experience with data collection tools. Participants will explore how various data types and mixed methods templates can produce insights into the design of a data flow in educational technology.
title: ProjectWeeks: Data Design Studio for AI-Powered EdTech

name: Project Weeks: Decision Education
content:
Each of the five days of the project week will be centered around one theme, which will be first introduced in the morning interactive lecture, followed by activities, group work and presentations. The topics explored will be:
1.	Introduction to the biases of decision making and the way in which they are empirically studied – introduction and brief historical overview of the field of decision making as investigated in evolutionary psychology, behavioural economics, social psychology, and computational cognitive science
2.	Decision-making as a teachable skill – introduces the program of Decision Education and the toolbox for improving decision making
3.	Communicating risk and uncertainty to make better medical and economic decisions – this day will explore how experts should information be presented to others by professionals so that they can make the best possible decisions, focusing on risk communication, which is the domain where most empirical data are available
4.	Making decisions in an online world: who can we trust? – this day will explore social decision making biases, spread of misinformation, and their consequences on partner choice, as well as wider political decision making, with a focus on online environments
5. Decision education in the classroom and in society – this class will focus on decision making in the context of education, but also on how governments are using insights from decision-making for designing policy
6.  The use of AI tools in decision-making: a double-edged sword
objective:
At the end of the project week, students will be able to:
1. To reflect on the limitations and potential biases of our own decision-making processes and outcomes. 
2. To brainstorm about we could overcome these biases and limitations, that is, how can we improve decision-making competence among university students. 
3. To discuss how a program for Decision Education could look like, that is able to empower students with the skills and dispositions essential to be able to learn actively, independently, and efficiently, make sound inferences, and take informed decisions.
prerequisites: English language fluency
title: Project week: Decision Education

name: Design Challenge: Addressing the Climate Crisis Through Gaming Simulation
content: Diese Designchallenge ist ein ambitioniertes Projekt mit dem Ziel, interaktive Planspiele (Gaming Simulations) zur Klimakrise in interdisziplinären Teams zu konzipieren. Obwohl die Klimakrise zu den drängendsten Herausforderungen unserer Zeit zählt, fehlt es bislang an motivierenden und lernwirksamen Lernumgebungen, die insbesondere Jugendliche und junge Erwachsene ansprechen – und sich zugleich für den Einsatz in Schule und Hochschule eignen.Planspiele (Gaming Simulations) bieten das Potenzial, diese Lücke zu schließen: Sie ermöglichen es jungen Menschen, sich in der Komplexität des Klimawandels besser zu orientieren und daraus konkrete, nachhaltige Handlungsoptionen abzuleiten. Ein durchdachtes, einsetzbares Planspiel kann darüber hinaus skalierbar verbreitet und langfristig in Bildungskontexte integriert werden. Die Designchallenge bietet Studierenden aller Fachrichtungen die Möglichkeit, an einer realen gesellschaftlichen Herausforderung zu arbeiten, neue Methoden kennenzulernen und die eigene Wirksamkeit im Team zu erleben.
objective:
Nach erfolgreicher Teilnahme an der Design Challenge sind die Studierenden in der Lage,

1. komplexe gesellschaftliche Herausforderungen wie die Klimakrise zu analysieren und zentrale Zielkonflikte (z. B. zwischen Ökologie, Ökonomie und sozialer Gerechtigkeit) zu benennen
2. Grundlagen der pädagogisch-psychologischen Lehr-Lernforschung zu beschreiben und auf die Entwicklung wirkungsvoller Lernumgebungen zu übertragen
3. didaktische Potenziale von Planspielen zu erläutern und gezielt für Bildungszwecke einzusetzen
4. verschiedene Typen von Planspielen (z. B. Entscheidungs-, Verhandlungs- und Rollenspiele) hinsichtlich Zielsetzung, Spielmechanik und Einsatzkontext zu unterscheiden und einzuordnen
5. einen spielbaren Prototyp eines Planspiels eigenständig und im Team zu konzipieren, umzusetzen und weiterzuentwickeln
6. aktuelle Gestaltungsprinzipien aus Game Design und Nachhaltigkeitsbildung praktisch anzuwenden
7. interdisziplinär und kollaborativ in heterogenen Teams zu arbeiten, eigene Perspektiven einzubringen und mit anderen konstruktiv zu verknüpfen
8. Feedbackprozesse aktiv zu gestalten, in den eigenen Entwicklungsprozess zu integrieren und kritisch-reflexiv damit umzugehen
9. eigene Wirksamkeit in einem offenen, kreativen Lernprozess zu erleben und zu reflektieren
10. wissenschaftlich fundierte Entscheidungen im Designprozess zu begründen und mit aktuellen Erkenntnissen zu verknüpfen (z. B. zur Wirkung von Simulationen auf Motivation, Handlungskompetenz oder Systemverständnis)
11. das entwickelte Planspiel in Bildungskontexte zu übertragen, Anwendungsmöglichkeiten zu reflektieren und Ansätze zur Weiterentwicklung zu formulieren
title: Design Challenge: Adressing the Climate Crisis through Gaming Simulation

name: Project Weeks: Developing AI-Powered Educational Interventions for an Attention-Aware Video Player
content:
Have you ever watched a lecture only to suddenly realize you were planning dinner instead of paying attention to the professor? This phenomenon, called mind wandering, can disrupt learning. But what if we had a video player to detect when our attention drifts and help us refocus?
In this project week, students will develop real-time AI-powered educational interventions for an existing attention-aware video player. Students will have the opportunity to design and implement adaptive support, like intermediate comprehension questions, directly into the video player that prompts learners to refocus. 
After an initial introduction to the topic and the existing video player tool, students will work independently, receiving feedback from instructors at various stages of development. To conclude, participants will conduct a small user study to evaluate the effectiveness of their interventions in improving learner attention and outcomes. This hands-on project offers a unique opportunity to merge education and computer science, allowing students to develop cutting-edge solutions that support attention in educational settings.
objective: By the end of this project week, students will understand how attention and mind wandering affect learning and how to design AI-powered interventions to address these challenges. They will gain hands-on experience implementing adaptive features in an attention-aware video player and using AI tools like ChatGPT. Additionally, they will learn to conduct small-scale user studies to evaluate their interventions and improve their ability to work on an interdisciplinary project.
prerequisites: Master’s students from the fields of Informatics, Data Science, Mechanical Engineering, Information Systems, Education Science
title: Project Week: Developing AI-Powered Educational Interventions for an Attention-Aware Video Player

name: Project Weeks: Media World and Media Use
content: Wie sich unsere Medienwelt entwickelt, ist eine Frage, die gesellschaftlich für uns alle eine tragende Rolle spielt. Die Studierenden erkunden, wie und wie viel ihrer Welt sie durch Medien wahrnehmen. Sie beschäftigen sich mit Voraussetzungen und Arbeitsweisen unterschiedlicher Medien. Sie reflektieren, wie und warum sie verschiedene Medien nutzen. Ihre eigenen Erfahrungen und ihr Wissen sind in dem Projektseminar die Basis, um eine zukünftige Medienwelt zu entwerfen – welche Wünsche richten sich an Medien, welche Funktionen sollen sie in Zukunft idealerweise erfüllen, welchen Einschränkungen sollen sie ggf. unterliegen? Welche Arten der Nutzung sind möglich, welche sind wünschenswert? Die Zukunftsentwürfe zur Medienwelt, welche die Studierenden zu diesen Fragen entwickeln, präsentieren und diskutieren sie zum Abschluss mit professionellen Kommunikatoren.
objective: Sie reflektieren, welche Rolle Medien in verschiedenen Kontexten spielen. Indem Sie selbst einen Zukunftsentwurf zur Medienwelt gestalten, bringen Sie Ihre Ideen und Ihre Lösungsansätze ein.
prerequisites: keine
title: Reflecting on the media world and media usage

name: Data Ethics and Governance
categories: Social and Political Aspects of Data Science
content:
This project week (11–15 January 2027) gives students the opportunity to collaborate with Local Contexts, under the leadership of experienced researchers, to address urgent challenges in the governance, sharing, and ethics linked to Indigenous data. Local Contexts (localcontext.org) is an Indigenous-led not for profit organization that works internationally to support Indigenous data sovereignty through an innovative system of data labelling. As an organization that delivers practical tools to support Indigenous aspirations for data governance, Local Contexts is seeking advice in developing a unique Local Contexts Dashboard to make more visible the vital connections and relationships between the varied users of the Local Contexts tools. These users include Indigenous communities, museums, libraries, archives and biodiversity data repositories and researchers. This project offers a rare chance for students and partners to engage in a shared space of theoretical and practical technical problem-solving with the goal of contributing to advancement in data ethics and Indigenous data sovereignty. 

The project adopts the format of a “data clinic,” which is an interactive problem-solving and teaching format designed to bridge theory and practice in the realm of data governance and ethics.  It creates an opportunity for both students and partners to enter a space of co-learning and problem-solving, and for students to make a real impact on embedding ethical principles around Indigenous data into database systems, guided by the Data Ethics team at the Chair of Philosophy and History of Science and Technology. The project also builds on the ground-breaking work done by the Ethical Data Initiative hosted at the TUM Think Tank. The project week will incorporate activities such as mini-lectures, expert talks, a data graphics workshop, and several Q&A sessions with a representative of the partner organisation. 

In sum: 
- Work with a leading Indigenous data sovereignty partners on real-world problems.
- Develop your talent as a next-generation researcher or practitioner with experience in data ethics. 
- Work intensively in a small group on problems with public interest stakes.
objective:
After completion of the course, students will be able to understand and apply core concepts and implications of data ethics, responsible data practices, and socially accountable data governance in practice. Students will gain experience in identifying and tackling ethical and social challenges and opportunities emerging from methods, tools, and practices of indigenous data governance, with a particular emphasis on supporting local communities in data governance and embedding data ethics into technical systems. 

Broadly, the project will equip students with the skills to understand and critically discuss current research on data ethics and governance, ways in which related challenges can be identified and tackled, and the wider impact of such challenges on society.  

It will allow students to collaboratively translate their interpretations and insights into responsible approaches and ways of working with data beyond academic discussions. 
 
The interactive workshop format further encourages collaboration and knowledge exchange between students with different disciplinary backgrounds. STEM and computer sciences students, for instance, will gain insight into larger ethical, social, and epistemic issues linked to their specialisations; while social sciences and politics students will acquire experience in analysing practical and technical aspects of data-work.
prerequisites: none
title: Data Ethics in Practice: Dashboarding Indigenous Data Sovereignty with Local Contexts

name: Society and Technology
categories: Social and Political Aspects of Data Science
content:
This course is designed to introduce non-social scientists to ‘the social’ and ‘society’. Before we get to the specific role of ‘data’ and ‘technology’ in society, we need to understand how people live together, how they interact and how that becomes meaningful to them. Understanding society is very different from understanding a technical system. 

So the course starts with an introduction to social science epistemology. How can we know and understand social phenomena? We then gallop through a set of core social theories that help us to understand the different perspectives onto ‘the social’. This will cover some 20th century white dudes, but also something a little more up-to-date and infused with feminism and postcolonial critique. 

Once we have the basics, we will begin to look into the specifics of data, technology and risk.
objective: You will learn to think about and understand social phenomena. This involves understanding social science epistemologies and important social theories. You will also be introduced to ways of thinking about the relationship between data, technology and society with a focus on risk. This course is an introductory course designed to enable you to decide whether this sort of research and focus is for you or not.
prerequisites: none
title: Understanding Society

name: Data Governance in Action
content: The ‘Data Governance in Action’ module focuses on the practical implementation of data governance principles in modern organizations. It encompasses an extensive range of crucial topics vital for comprehending and executing effective data governance strategies. The module commences with an introduction to the data governance concepts and their pivotal significance in the digital economy. Students will delve into the legal and regulatory frameworks for data management, including GDPR, the EU Data Act, and the EU Data Governance Act to ensure adherence to regulations and best practices.
title: Data Governance in Action

name: Responsibility in the Engineering Profession
categories: Social and Political Aspects of Data Science
content:
On the one hand, the successful implementation of an engineering project is essentially based on technical expertise. On the other hand, a wide range of other competencies, such as efficient project management, goal-oriented personnel management, conflict management, etc., are necessary, for example, to successfully implement a construction project operationally. Social competencies, i.e. ethical values such as trust, responsibility, mutual recognition of rights and obligations, etc., which also contribute significantly to the success of an engineering project, are often overlooked. In addition to a legal anchoring, these normative concepts also contain moral-ethical contents, ethical norms and values, which will be presented and systematically elaborated in this interdisciplinary introductory seminar and tested on practical case studies, i.e. a successful realization of construction projects.
All participants are expected to give one (group-) presentation during the course.
prerequisites: NO special philosophical knowledge is necessary!
title: Responsibility in the Engineering Profession. Applied Ethics for Engineers

name: Academic Prompt Engineering and Management: a Reflexive Introduction
content:
This module builds on the lecture and provides students from all parts of Technical University Munich with a solidification of knowledge concerning the use of generative AI. The course combines hands-on training in effective prompting techniques with an exploration of the legal, ethical, and societal responsibility issues surrounding the use of LLMs for text generation.
Through a two-day interactive seminar, students will deepen their knowledge by using practical skills in prompt engineering while developing a nuanced understanding of the broader implications of this rapidly evolving technology. Topics covered include:
• Application of techniques for prompt engineering in text generation using LLMs, including methods for measuring prompt effectiveness, advanced techniques, and addressing issues like hallucinations and ensuring accuracy.
• Implementation of responsible development and deployment of LLMs, focusing on selecting appropriate models, identifying and mitigating biases, ensuring transparency, and evaluating decision-making capacity.
• In-depth exploration of human-computer interaction with LLMs, including decision-making processes, the future of work in the context of LLM-powered text generation, and their applications in academic research.
• Considerations for designing and evaluating large language models, focusing on performance, fairness, transparency, and robustness.
• Application of requirements of intellectual property, copyright, fairness, diversity and other legal and ethical issues related to LLM-generated text.
• The transformative potential and rapid progress of LLMs, highlighting their ability to reshape interactions with technology and information across various domains.
objective:
Upon successful completion of this module, students will be able to:

• Describe and apply techniques for prompt engineering in text generation using large language models (LLMs), including methods for measuring prompt effectiveness, advanced techniques, and strategies for addressing issues like hallucinations and ensuring accuracy.
• Explain the importance of responsible development and deployment of LLMs, and demonstrate the ability to select appropriate models, identify and mitigate biases, ensure transparency, and evaluate the decision-making capacity of LLMs.
• Analyze human-computer interaction with LLMs, including decision-making processes, and discuss the future of work in the context of LLM-powered text generation and their applications in academic research.
• Evaluate the design and performance of large language models, focusing on key considerations such as fairness, transparency, and robustness.
• Identify and discuss intellectual property, copyright, and other legal and ethical issues related to LLM-generated text.
• Assess the transformative potential and rapid progress of LLMs, and explain their ability to reshape interactions with technology and information across various domains.
prerequisites: None
title: Academic Prompt Engineering and Management: a Reflexive Introduction

name: Academic Prompt Engineering and Management: Responsible Use in Action
content:
This module builds on the lecture and provides students from all parts of Technical University Munich with a solidification of knowledge concerning the use of generative AI. The course combines hands-on training in effective prompting techniques with an exploration of the legal, ethical, and societal responsibility issues surrounding the use of LLMs for text generation.
Through a two-day interactive seminar, students will deepen their knowledge by using practical skills in prompt engineering while developing a nuanced understanding of the broader implications of this rapidly evolving technology. Topics covered include:
• Application of techniques for prompt engineering in text generation using LLMs, including methods for measuring prompt effectiveness, advanced techniques, and addressing issues like hallucinations and ensuring accuracy.
• Implementation of responsible development and deployment of LLMs, focusing on selecting appropriate models, identifying and mitigating biases, ensuring transparency, and evaluating decision-making capacity.
• In-depth exploration of human-computer interaction with LLMs, including decision-making processes, the future of work in the context of LLM-powered text generation, and their applications in academic research.
• Considerations for designing and evaluating large language models, focusing on performance, fairness, transparency, and robustness.
• Application of requirements of intellectual property, copyright, fairness, diversity and other legal and ethical issues related to LLM-generated text.
• The transformative potential and rapid progress of LLMs, highlighting their ability to reshape interactions with technology and information across various domains.
objective:
Upon successful completion of this module, students will be able to:

• Evaluate novel prompt engineering techniques for text generation using large language models (LLMs), including developing new methods for measuring prompt effectiveness and designing strategies to address issues like hallucinations and ensure accuracy.
• Evaluate and critique the responsible development and deployment of LLMs, including designing frameworks for model selection, bias mitigation, transparency assurance, and assessment of LLMs' decision-making capacity.
• Synthesize research on human-computer interaction with LLMs, including analyzing decision-making processes and predicting future trends in work and academic research in the context of LLM-powered text generation.
• Design and conduct experiments to assess the performance of large language models, with a focus on developing new metrics and methodologies for evaluating fairness, transparency, and robustness.
• Analyze and propose solutions for complex intellectual property, copyright, and ethical dilemmas related to LLM-generated text, considering various stakeholder perspectives and potential societal impacts.
• Formulate and defend hypotheses about the long-term transformative potential of LLMs, including creating scenarios for how they might reshape interactions with technology and information across various domains.
prerequisites: Students should be familiar with the contents of the introductory module SOT53404.
title: Academic Prompt Engineering and Management: Responsible Use in Action

name: Open Data - Open Science (Introduction)
categories: Social and Political Aspects of Data Science
content:
The module is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the principles and practices of openness in scientific research and data management. The course is structured to highlight the transformative potential of open science, in particular open access to publications, open research data, and open source for science in society, emphasizing not only aspects of research integrity or innovation (such as reproducibility), but also aspects of democratizing access and use of knowledge. It also aims to foster students’ understanding of the Open Science movement, its impact on science and society, and, more generally, current transformation in research practices and governance. The module builds around the research conducted within the PHIL_OS project (www.opensciencestudies.eu), one of the leading research groups worldwide working on these issues, and therefore focuses on the cutting-edge of research on Open Science. Through case studies, students will explore foundational concepts such as the political economy of scientific knowledge production and the significance of open science initiatives. The course will also cover key topics including open source projects, open infrastructures, and citizen science, illustrated with real-world case studies to demonstrate their impact on various fields.
In terms of disciplinary domain, we will discuss emerging research within the fields of philosophy, history and social studies of science and technology, as well as meta-research (sometimes also referred to as “research on research”). Topics encompass, but are not be limited to: the reproducibility crisis; information quality; inequity and injustice across research environments; data-intensive technologies and AI; data management; cooperation and coordination within and across scientific institutions; citizen science and public science; science governance; scientific modelling and epistemology. See the detailed schedule for more details. Attendees are required to attend sessions regularly, study the readings for each week in advance of the meeting, and come prepared for discussion.
objective:
By the end of this module, students will be able to: 
- describe the principles of open science and open (research) data. 
- understand the impact of open initiatives like the Human Genome Project across several societal domains, such as research, politics, education, economy, security 
- apply open science practices in their own research fields
title: Introduction to Open Data - Open Science

name: Applied Philosophy of AI: Public Dialog on Future Practices
content:
AI agents are often predicted to be the next great advancement in digital technology. However, there’s considerable uncertainty about the nature of AI agents and how they can best complement human agency. 

This seminar builds on the rich philosophical discussion of agency to clarify fundamental questions about AI agents, including: What is an agent, and what constitutes agency? How do intentionality, consciousness, will, and understanding contribute to agency? Can AI systems be agents in their own right, or do they necessarily depend on human agency? What are their strengths and fundamental limitations? How can cooperation among agents create new forms of agency, and how can AI agents best complement human agency?

We’ll explore these and related questions through groundbreaking philosophical texts chosen by students from a curated list. Students can also suggest other texts that interest them. The seminar combines regular in-person meetings with exchanges involving SAP employees who work with AI agents in real business contexts.
objective:
Upon successful completion of this seminar, students will be able to:
• Analyze classical and contemporary philosophical texts
• Describe key arguments from ongoing philosophical debates about AI and agency
• Distinguish between features of agency and meaning, and explain how they relate to computation
• Explain how AI agents can influence human thought, emotion, and behavior
• Outline the implications of deploying AI agents in business contexts
• Present philosophical ideas to a public audience that includes industry participants
title: Agentic AI, Agents, and Shared Agency

name: Responsible Quantum Computing
content: The module focuses on practices of responsible research and innovation in quantum computing. Using selected case studies from science, politics and industry, they explore different strategies for fostering responsible innovation and critically engage in them.
objective: Upon successful completion of this module, students will be able to evaluate how innovation processes in quantum computing can be designed more responsibly. In addition to this hands-on perspective, students will be able to analyze why and how traditional modes of responsible research and innovation can be criticized in emerging technological fields.
prerequisites: There are no specific prerequisites for participation in this module. Basic knowledge of technology, sociology, or innovation research is advantageous. A strong interest in interdisciplinary perspectives on technology and society is recommended, as the module combines various methodological and theoretical approaches.
title: Responsible Quantum Computing

name: The Future of Data Governance
content:
The course provides comprehensive overview overimportant aspects of data governance and data law. 
The aim is to train students in socially responsible use of data and thus, provide them with a good understanding of the most important areas of data law. Data law includes not only the particularly important area of data protection law, but also IT security law, the emerging law of data sharing, data access and open data law. Today, data protection law has become an important and indispensable prerequisite for activities in organizations. Particularly in business, the GDPR has become a "boardroom issue" due to the relatively high fines, which can be as high as 4% of annual turnover for a data protection breach, so basic knowledge in this field is of great benefit. Likewise, IT security law is enjoying growing importance. However, modern data law goes much further than these areas. Especially in the public sector, but also in the area of research data, there are increasingly far-reaching transparency obligations and obligations to publish. Data sharing infrastructures are also under legislative discussion, particularly as a result of the Data Governance Act. In addition, there is an intensive discussion about data access obligations.
objective:
Upon successful completion of this module, students should be able to:
•	learn basic terms and get a comprehensible overview of these dynamic matters. In each case, questions that are relevant for students and that they can ideally apply will be discussed in greater depth. 
•	reflect on specific regulatory choices and their intended and unintended impacts
•	develop problem awareness and the ability to express themselves.
•	reflect on the respective choices made in a legal argument and link it to important concepts of constitutional magnitude
•	acquire basic knowledge of law and legal methods that can also be of use to them in other contexts and that are very profitable for graduates of TUM in higher employment. However, this knowledge is to be woven into the course in such a way that students discuss central questions such as interpretation or the European theory of legal sources where they are relevant. In this way, the basic educational mandate is also fulfilled, which does justice to the guiding principle of independent-thinking human-centered engineering.
prerequisites: No previous knowledge expected
title: The Future of Data Governance: Sharing, Accessing, Securing and Protecting Data

name: Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence: Key Readings
categories: Social and Political Aspects of Data Science
content:
To what extent may phenomenology contribute to a better understanding of the basic concepts, presuppositions, and aims of AI? One of phenomenology’s main contributions to science in general (i.e., not only with respect to AI), is to clarify the basic concepts and statements of the respective field of investigation. It does so not by providing explicit definitions, but by explaining these basic concepts and statements in a way that does not amount to a reduction to some indefinable concepts. The phenomenological approach, as Gödel once put it with respect to Husserl’s method, is a way of “focusing more sharply on the concept concerned by directing our attention […] onto our own acts in the use of these concepts, onto our powers in carrying out our acts, […]. [It is] a procedure or technique that should produce in us a new state of consciousness in which we describe in detail the basic concepts we use in our thought, or grasp other basic concepts hitherto unknown to us”.
On which assumptions is the AI’s conception of the mind as an information-processing system based? Is intentionality an exclusivity of minds, or could a suitably programmed computer also be able to exhibit intentionality? Can the mind and all phenomena associated with it be reduced to a set of mechanical transformations or computations? Based on the discussion of various classical works from the field of philosophy of artificial intelligence (e.g., Dreyfus, Turing, Searle, among others), this course aims at shedding light to these and other fundamental philosophical questions concerning the relationship between AI and the human mind from a phenomenological perspective.
objective:
Upon completion of the course, students shall:
• be familiarised with classic works and discussions within the field of philosophy of AI
• be able to analyse philosophical texts and arguments concerning the philosophy of AI
• understand the historical developments leading to the many philosophical questions raised by AI and related technologies.
title: Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence. Classical Readings in the Phenomenology of AI

name: Applied Philosophy of Quantum Theory
content: Quantum computers are expected to progress from today’s noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices (NISQ) to fault-tolerant architectures. Alongside this hardware development, advances in quantum algorithms exploit superposition, interference, and entanglement to speed up certain computational tasks. This course introduces the foundations of quantum information and computation and develops core quantum algorithmic ideas in several contexts – from search and amplitude amplification to techniques used in quantum learning. We will explore how these algorithms operate, what resources they require, and when they can offer practical or theoretical advantages over classical approaches.
objective: This module is organized around a set of conceptual questions presented by quantum computing, quantum machine learning, and optimization. By the end of the course, students will be able to explain the key concepts of quantum physics leveraged in quantum computations and learn about selected quantum algorithms and their applications in quantum machine learning and optimization. The module also explores foundational and philosophical questions in quantum physics, highlighting their close relationship to the conceptual framework of quantum computation.
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of Python and linear algebra.
title: Quantum Information Meets Artificial Intelligence. From Foundations to Applications

name: Actors, Environments and Technologies – Experimenting with Ways of Knowing and Doing STS
content:
Water is a planetary challenge that no single discipline can address alone. This Project takes water as its starting point, not just as a resource or a technical problem, but as an object of future-making that is scientific, political, and cultural all at once.

How can we explore water beyond the methods of our own discipline? How can we talk about water across disciplinary boundaries, and with publics who hold their own knowledge and stories about water?

We will discuss global water insecurity alongside emerging technological interventions, from atmospheric water harvesting to lunar ice extraction, to ask how different fields imagine, design, and contest water futures, and what gets left out when only one discipline does the imagining.

The course introduces Speculative Fabulation (SF), a creative-analytical framework developed by feminist Science and Technology Studies scholar Donna Haraway, as a method for interdisciplinary inquiry. 

Students from STEMM and design are invited to treat it as a practice that critically engages with scientific and societal approaches to water futures. Through theoretical input, artistic workshops, and project-based work, students reflect on their disciplinary assumptions, collaborate across fields, and produce speculative interventions that bring scientific expertise into dialogue with storytelling. The course cultivates competencies beyond technical knowledge, including critical thinking, tolerance for ambiguity, and communication across disciplines. By the end of the Project Week, students will have contributed a digital artifact to a shared archive demonstrating how scientific knowledge can be combined with speculative storytelling to reimagine water futures.
objective:
Upon completion of the module, students are able to 

    Understand interdisciplinary water research beyond technical knowledge 

    Critically engage with scientific and societal approaches to water 

    Understand methods in Social Science 

    Apply critical thinking to their own fields of study 

    Expand their methods of writing for academic and non-academic purposes 

    Engage with creative methods for science communication and communication across disciplines 

    Create creative output of scientific content
title: Exploring Water Otherwise: The Art of Storytelling in the Anthropocene

name: Project: Science, Art and Society - New Ways of Communicating Knowledge
content:
If an experience is worth more than a thousand words, why is science communication often confined to traditional, straightforward, and sometimes even paternalistic explanations of scientific phenomena?

This workshop offers a hands-on approach to responsible science communication, equipping students with the skills to design and implement their own experimental programs for creating participatory and engaging experiences. While participation and engagement are key concepts in responsible science communication theories, these must extend beyond theoretical frameworks and be brought into the practical realm. Students will learn how to move beyond mere knowledge transfer of scientific concepts and instead create compelling narratives and immersive experiences that foster the active production of knowledge.

The course provides a comprehensive learning encounter, including two visits to the Deutsches Museum and two moderated concept development sessions for students to develop their own experimental programs. During the sessions at the Deutsches Museum, students will participate in two experimental visitor programs (“Alchemy” and “Microchips under the magnifying glass ”), allowing them to observe, analyse, and reflect on established science communication strategies in action. For their final project, students will design and present a short experimental program that showcases the knowledge and skills they have acquired.

This initiative empowers students to become responsible and innovative science communicators, bridging the gap between their scientific disciplines and the public in a truly participatory and engaging way.
objective:
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:
- Identify and apply responsible science communication strategies.
- Communicate complex scientific and technical concepts in practical and engaging ways.
- Develop innovative, interactive, and experimental methods for science participation and engagement.
- Design and execute public participation and engagement programs.
prerequisites: No
title: Hands-On SciCom: Experiment-Driven Science Communication

name: History and Remembrance
content:
"Nie wieder!“ Die Verbrechen des Nazi-Regimes sind eines der dunkelsten Kapitel der deutschen Geschichte. Die KZ-Gedenkstätte Dachau erinnert nicht nur an das unfassbare Leid der Verfolgten und Ermordeten infolge des Nazi-Regimes, sondern ist auch Appell an die Verantwortung der nachfolgenden Generationen, eine Wiederholung eines jeglichen totalitär-barbarischen Regimes zu verhindern.

In Kooperation und unter Leitung des Max Mannheimer Studienzentrums in Dachau widmet sich die zweitägige Veranstaltung diesen Aufgaben in Form eines geführten Rundgangs und Workshop. Zum einen zeigt sie das Leben und Werk von Menschen, die, bei allen Differenzen, eines miteinander verbindet: die Gefangenschaft im Konzentrationslager Dachau. Unterschiedlichste (historische) Dokumente, wie autobiografische Zeugnisse, Fotografien und Filmsequenzen, eröffnen Perspektiven auf das Leben der Menschen während der Zeit des Nationalsozialismus und darüber hinaus. Zum anderen setzt sie sich mit der Notwendigkeit einer Erinnerungskultur, mit den unterschiedlichen Phasen der Konfrontation mit der Zeit des Nationalsozialismus in der Bundesrepublik auseinander. 
Anhand einzelner Gruppen ehem. Verfolgter wird u.a. aufgezeigt, wie Marginalisierung und Diskriminierung auch in der Bundesrepublik weiterwirkten.
objective: Die Studierenden sind in der Lage, die politisch-sozialen Kontexte von spezifischen historischen Ereignisse zu identifizieren, individuelle Lebesläufe und Äußerungen von Zeitzeugen im Zusammenhang mit den Ereignissen und deren Kontexten einzuordnen sowie Aspekte von Erinnerungskultur und kollektiver Vergangenheitsbewältigung kritisch zu diskutieren.
prerequisites: Keine Voraussetzungen.
title: Discrimination, Persecution and Extinction:  Dachau Concentration Camp in History & Present

name: Intercultural Encounters
content:
What does “international” really mean? Beyond stereotypes, we can discover both fascinating diversity and surprising similarities. 
In this seminar, German and international students come together to learn, exchange, and experience cultural diversity in an open and authentic way. Workshops, cultural events, and group projects provide space to explore differences, reflect on them, and build common ground. 
  
Participants strengthen their intercultural sensitivity, learn to navigate challenges in diverse teams, and develop skills for respectful and constructive collaboration. 

  
Key questions we will explore include: 
•	How do unconscious biases and stereotypes shape perception and interaction? 
•	How can I deal with irritating situations in intercultural settings? 
•	How do people build trust and give constructive feedback? 
•	What skills are crucial for intercultural teamwork?
objective:
After the course, participants will be able to… 
•	identify cultural standards and reflect on their own background 
•	recognize and address stereotyping in intercultural contexts 
•	deal more constructively with cultural differences and conflicts 
•	work effectively in diverse teams towards shared goals 
•	use cultural events as opportunities for dialogue and perspective-taking
prerequisites: Good English language skills (level B2)
title: Come Together! - Inter/Cultural Practice for Locals, Foreigners and World Inhabitants

name: Project Week: Creative Mind Change. A Creativity Workshop
content: Fünf ganztägige Workshops führen mit Experteninput und Diskussionen in Aspekte künstlerischen Arbeitens ein. In Kooperation mit der Kunstakademie Bad Reichenhall vermitteln drei Dozenierende den Teilnehmenden unterschiedliche kreative Praktiken (Werkstattcharakter vor Ort an der TUM), die praktisch erprobt (künstlerische Medien), theoretisch in Diskussion und Vortrag vermittelt und in Form von Gruppnarbeit und Präsentation vertieft werden. Inhalt und Ziel des Projekts ist die Anwendung der erworbenen Kenntnisse auf KI-Modelle wie etwa DALL-2, um Möglichkeiten und Grenzen neuer Kreativitätspotentiale in der Kommunikation von Technologie und genuin humaner Kreativität auszuloten.
objective:
Nach der Teilnahme sind die Studierenden in der Lage …
- die eigenen kreativen Potentiale zu erkennen,
- die Abhängigkeiten von bisherigen Erfahrungs- und Denkmustern zu verstehen
- die erworbenen künstlerischen bzw. kreativen Methoden anzuwenden, um komplexe Phänomene abzubilden und hieraus konkrete Handlungsoptionen zu entwickeln.
- Coping Strategien hinsichtlich (scheinbar) divergenter Themen, Begriffe, Vorstellungen, Handlungsmodelle und Produkte zu entwickeln.
title: Project Week: Creative Mind Change. A Creativity Workshop

name: Stories and Histories. Experience Literature in Its Historical Context.
content:
Was bietet uns heute (noch) die Beschäftigung mit Persönlichkeiten aus der Vergangenheit? Was fangen wir mit ihren Texten an, was leiten wir daraus für unsere Gegenwart ab? Am Beispiel von Erika Mann (1905-1969), dem „kühnen Kind“, wie Literaturnobelpreisträger Thomas Mann (1875-1955) seine älteste Tochter bewundernd nannte, stellen wir uns diesen Fragen und versuchen, uns damit der Geschichte gegenüber zu positionieren. 

Erika Manns Leben verläuft geradezu exemplarisch an den entscheidenden Schnittstellen des 20. Jahrhunderts entlang: von der Rebellin und „neuen Frau“ der 1920er Jahre über die kompromisslose Streiterin für Frieden und Freiheit in den 1930/40er Jahren bis zur konservativen Nachlassverwalterin für den Vater und ihren Bruder Klaus nach dem Zweiten Weltkrieg. Nie wollte sie sich dem „Familienfluch Schreiben“ beugen, eignete sich ihn jedoch auf ganz eigene Weise an. 
Schlagworte wie Queerness, Cultural Clash, Exilerfahrung oder Female Heritage können auf sie und ihr vielseitiges Werk ausprobiert werden, greift sie in ihren mitunter sehr modern klingenden Schriften Themen auf, die auch für uns heute (wieder/ noch) aktuell sind – politisch, gesellschaftlich, kulturell. 

Das gemeinsame Lesen und Diskutieren ausgewählter Texte soll den Zugang zu Erika Manns Lebenswelt erfahrbar machen. Zugleich soll deutlich werden, inwieweit die persönliche Perspektive die Bewertung der Vergangenheit beeinflusst. Durch das Schreiben und Referieren eigener Texte, die von Erika Manns Werk und/ oder ihrer Biographie inspiriert sind, werden diese Beobachtungen auf einer weiteren Ebene reflektiert.

Erika Manns literarisches Schaffen umfasst Feuilletons, Reiseberichte, Glossen, Kabaretttexte, Reden, politische Bücher über Hitler und den Nationalsozialismus sowie Kinderbücher und ein riesiges Konvolut Briefe. Es ist größtenteils digital über das Literaturarchiv Monacensia zugänglich. Ein Besuch dort wird vorstellen, wie ein solches Erbe betreut und für nachfolgende Generationen bewahrt, aber auch wie damit recherchiert und gearbeitet wird.
objective: Die exemplarische Beschäftigung mit Biographie, Werk und Wirken einer historischen Persönlichkeit ermöglicht, diese zeitgeschichtlich einzuordnen und ihre Bedeutung für die Gegenwart zu hinterfragen. Die subjektive und kontextuelle Prägung eines solchen Vorgehens wird herausgearbeitet. Zugleich eröffnen literarische Schreibübungen eine neue Reflexionsebene.
prerequisites:
Keine – außer der Bereitschaft, Texte zu lesen, zu diskutieren und selbst zu verfassen.
Deutschlernende sind herzlich willkommen. Da der Wechsel der Sprache in Erika Manns Biographie eine große Rolle spielt, wird das Einbringen entsprechender eigener Erfahrungen begrüßt. Unterrichtssprache ist Deutsch.
title: Stories and Histories: Erika Mann - a "Bold Child" of Her Time?

name: Game Jam. Reflecting Science, Technology and Society through Game Design
categories: Studiengangsübergreifende Angebote der Carl von Linde-Akademie
Studiengangsübergreifende Angebote der Carl von Linde-Akademie
Studiengangsübergreifende Angebote der Carl von Linde-Akademie
content:
This course offers an interdisciplinary setting in which the participants develop their own videogame concept (no programming required) — it is therefore aimed at all students, e.g. from the STEM sciences, Games Engineering and the School of Social Sciences and Technology.

The students will be introduced to the social science perspective on STEM topics and the creative potential for reflection of video games, e.g. worldbuilding, storytelling and decision-making. Based on these inputs, the students develop their game-concept thematizing a STEM topic while enabling the creative potential of games to integrate societal and ethical aspects.
objective: The students are able to identify and discuss societal dimensions of STEM topics.
title: A Different Kind of Game Jam! Reflecting Science, Technology and Society through Game Design

name: Project: Ethics of Responsibility in the Field of Interdisciplinary Research Activities
content:
This project week contributes to the big picture of our sustainable future. It will enable to interact with students of different study lines in order to prepare yourself for the complex challenges of tomorrow.
Our “Philosophy” inspires you individually to ask the core questions of life and helps you to find your own responses. How would you like to live in the future? What tasks are needed to overcome barriers in mind and matter? 
•	Why is a great plant variety valuable for our society? How can ethical aspects of biodiversity politics contribute to our sustainable future.  Environmental ethics promotes and enhances the ethical debate in biodiversity communication.
•	Non human animals are valued “partners” within our society. What happens to our habits and interactions with the growing scientific evidence that a wide range of animals, including all vertebrates and many invertebrates, are likely conscious and are able to subjectively experience the world.
We will combine real case scenarios from natural sciences with methods and perspectives from the social sciences.
The chosen case studies should help you to participate in ongoing discussions and will support you to develop guiding principles towards certain topics.
Wild life management for example is a topic that involves many different stakeholders and perspectives. It makes it important to rethink frameworks and guidelines from the “generalized” view. 
In order to combine the theoretical dimension of the argumentation scenarios with clear practical options for everyday life we will go into “field” work and have discussions with experts in theoretical and practical professions.
objective:
Upon successful completion of this module, students are able to:
•	identify different research perspectives of different disciplines, their abilities, opportunities and limitations.
•	understand the complexity of research in the interrelationship of humans, nature and technology in an inter- and transdisciplinary perspective.
•	identify specific normative conflicts in selected fields of techno-sciences and society (e.g. technological innovation vs. ethical acceptance in society in case studies).
•	analyze normative conflicts and their possible ethical implications.
•	evaluate these conflicts ethically and apply them to specific current projects (e.g. environment, ecosystem, interrelationship between nature and culture, etc.).
•	develop a problem-solving strategy for a particular interdisciplinary project (e.g. ethics commission within non-human and human centered).
•	present their findings in a clear and concise manner
prerequisites: No
title: Project:

name: Utopias and Dystopias in Culture, Literature and Film
content:
What would an ideal society look like? What political order and what laws would this utopian state have to be based on? And when does a utopia become a dystopia? 
In this interdisciplinary seminar we will look at various fictional utopian texts and discuss real-world concepts and attempts to create ideal societies. In addition to different utopias, we will also look at the representation of dystopias in different media (novels, films, computer games) and examine the role of science and technology in both genres. Additionally, participants will work in groups to design their own utopian and dystopian societies and stories.
objective:
Students read literary texts from different eras, watch films and other media relevant to the topic and analyze them according to previously discussed criteria and methods. They research current discourses on the topic of the course and critically analyze them. 
Students also learn how to create and present an academic poster.
prerequisites: None apart from the willingness to read and discuss the texts.
title: From "New Atlantis" to "Blade Runner" - Utopias and Dystopias in Culture, Literature and Film

name: Arts & Technology. A Practice-oriented Introduction to Applied Cultural Studies
content:
Um 1900 entwickelte sich Barcelona zu einem der dynamischsten Kulturzentren Europas. Zwischen industriellem Aufbruch, dem rasanten Wachstum der Stadt und sozialen Konflikten entstand hier der katalanische Modernisme – eine außergewöhnliche Kunstbewegung, die Architektur, Malerei, Design und Literatur umfasste. 
Dabei ging es um das Ausloten von traditionellen Aspekten, modernen Impulsen und der Suche nach einer katalanischen Identität. Die Ausstellung "Barcelona moderna. Von Gaudí bis Picasso" in der Kunsthalle München widmet sich den künstlerischen Entwicklungen der Stadt zwischen 1880 und 1914. 
In der Veranstaltung werden wir über eine theoretisch-historische Einführung und Kurzreferaten zu den ausgestellten Werken ins Barcelona um 1900 eintauchen. Ein gemeinsamer Ausstellungsrundgang mit Hintergrundinformationen zur kuratorischen Arbeit vermittelt verschiedene Aspekte der Ausstellungspraxis. Im Anschluss wird ein Reiseführer mit den Highlights der Stadt erstellt.
objective: Nach der Teilnahme sind die Studierenden in der Lage, eigenständig ein kurzes Referat zu einem Kunstwerk zu halten und einen Kunst-Reiseführer zu entwerfen. Sie haben die grundlegenden Fähigkeiten für eine Bildbeschreibung und kunsthistorische Kontextualisierung des Werkes erworben. Außerdem erhielten sie Einblicke in die kuratorische Arbeit und das Konzipieren einer Ausstellung.
prerequisites: Interesse an Kunst und Kultur, Museumsbesuche, aktive Mitarbeit
title: Barcelona moderna. From Gaudí to Picasso. The Exhibition at the Kunsthalle Munich

- Identify and apply responsible science communication strategies.
- Communicate complex scientific and technical concepts in practical and engaging ways.
- Develop innovative, interactive, and experimental methods for science participation and engagement.
- Design and execute public participation and engagement programs.
prerequisites: No

name: Science Meets Fiction. Experiencing Literature in the Context of Science, Technology and Society
content: „As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams he found himself transformed in his bed into a gigantic insect.“ Franz Kafka’s opening sentence to „The Metamorphosis“ captures something essential about literature: its transformative power. Literature allows us to adopt unusal perspectives and to become someone or something else. In this participatory reading and writing workshop, we will explore this transformative power of literature through texts featuring unusual protagonists, perspectives, and worlds. We follow a nose through nineteenth-century St. Petersburg; marvel with a fox at the appearance of a strange creature called a shopping mall; or witness a woman’s transformation into a plant.Inspired by these stories, participants write their own texts from unexpected perspectives, which might include topics from their field of studies: How would quantum particles tell stories? What does the world of a molecule look like? What if the coronavirus were to tell its version of the pandemic? The workshop concludes with a small public reading.
objective: After completing the course, students will be able to understand and examine literary texts in terms of their transformative potential. Through discussions, they will reflect on and develop their own perspectives on the literary texts and the questions they raise. Through creative writing assignments, they will learn to view their own fields of study from a different perspective.
title: Becoming Other. The Transformative Power of Literature

name: Mankind and Nature. Philosophical Approaches
content:
"Die Natur verhandelt nicht. Wer versucht, sie zu ignorieren, wird unerbittlich bestraft." - So Anfang 2021 ein Spiegel-Kommentar. Was für ein Naturbild? Müssen wir Natur unbedingt pseudomythisch verklären, wenn wir sie nicht gerade als reines Objekt wissenschaftlich erforschen oder technisch ausnutzen? Wie lässt sich Natur denken?

Seit ihren Anfängen versuchte die Philosophie Natur zu begreifen. Die klassischen Begriffe physis und natura wurden in neueren Zeiten erweitert durch Umwelt, Ökosystem, Landschaft, Wildnis. Wie weit gehen philosophische Konzepte über die alltäglichen Verständnisse von Natur hinaus? Was verraten sie uns über das jeweilige Naturbild des Menschen? Und: Ermöglichen sie es, aktuelle Phänomene besser zu verstehen? Wenn es zum Beispiel um Naturkatastrophen, Umweltzerstörung, Greenwashing, Ökotourismus oder Bio-Produkte geht?

Im Seminar werden sowohl geläufige Naturbilder analysiert als auch philosophische Naturkonzepte vorgestellt, um sie abschließend in Gruppenprojekten mit aktuellen Herausforderungen in Wissenschaft, Technologie und Gesellschaft zu konfrontieren.
objective:
Nach der erfolgreichen Teilnahme an den Modulveranstaltungen sind die Studierenden in der Lage
- mindestens eine naturphilosophische Position in ausgewählten Aspekten darzustellen.
- wesentliche naturphilosophische Aussagen eines naturphilosophischen Textes zu identifizieren.
- Beziehungen zu heutigen wissenschafts- oder technikphilosophischen Problemen herzustellen.
- Teilaspekte des in den Natur- und Ingenieurwissenschaften jeweils vorausgesetzten Naturbegriffs aus einer bestimmten naturphilosophischen Perspektive zu charakterisieren
title: Back to Nature? Philosophical Perspectives on the Troubled Relationship between Nature and Mankind

This course offers an interdisciplinary setting in which the participants develop their own videogame concept (no programming required) — it is therefore aimed at all students, e.g. from the STEM sciences, Games Engineering and the School of Social Sciences and Technology.

The students will be introduced to the social science perspective on STEM topics and the creative potential for reflection of video games, e.g. worldbuilding, storytelling and decision-making. name: Current Issues in Cybersecurity Law
content: While software and software development were largely unregulated for a long time and private standardization set the security standards, the regulation of cybersecurity has experienced a new dynamic in recent years. Based on European regulations and directives, we can currently speak of the emergence of a new area of law: cybersecurity law. Following this dynamic is not easy, neither for computer scientists nor for lawyers. The seminar will first examine the basic approaches and requirements of European software regulation. In addition to fundamental institutions such as ENISA, which was created by the Cybersecurity Act, the NIS-2 Directive and the Cyber Resilience Act will be examined in particular. In the area of national law, the seminar will focus on the regulation of critical infrastructures and other sector-specific security requirements in business and administration, the planned comprehensive revision of the BSI Act in 2025 and the criminal law pitfalls of IT security research.

name: Data, Medicine & Law: The Legal Foundations of Digitalized Medicine
content: While state-of-the-art technologies such as AI systems and robotic procedures are being used in healthcare, in many areas it lags significantly behind the digital standard in other areas of life – for example, where fax machines are still used for data transmission. Based on the concept of a “data cycle,” the seminar examines the legal basis for the collection and storage of health data, the structure and regulation of data rooms, and access to this data in the context of data-driven and personalized medicine. The seminar focuses in particular on the requirements of data protection and IT security law as well as product safety law for software in the healthcare sector, the legal framework for data infrastructures, and access to health data for research and innovation. The seminar analyzes the interactions between technical developments and legal regulation and discusses the extent to which legal frameworks can promote, control, or inhibit innovation in the field of digitalized medicine.

name: The Judge and his Hacker
content: Im November 2022 hat das Unternehmen OpenAI den Prototyp eines KI basierten Chatbot namens „ChatGPT“ veröffentlicht. Seitdem wurden von vielen (Big-Tech)-Unternehmen zahlreiche weitere Large Language Models (LLMs) entwickelt. Ihre Fähigkeiten und die Auswirkungen auf verschiedene Bereiche des gesellschaftlichen Lebens werden seither virulent diskutiert, insbesondere ihr Einsatz in (Hochschul-)Prüfungen. Ziel des Seminars „Der Richter und sein Hacker“ ist es, den Studierenden ein Verständnis für die Verwendung von KI-generierten Texten zu vermitteln und ihnen beizubringen, wie man diese Texte kritisch bewerten und analysieren kann. Dazu werden auch externe Referenten („KI-Experten“) eingeladen. Im Rahmen des Seminars werden die Studierenden mit LLM-Tools Texte zu Themen des Digitalrechts erstellen. Hierbei sollen sie lernen, wie man die KI-generierten Texte interpretieren und bewerten kann, um zu erkennen, ob sie für eine bestimmte Anwendung geeignet sind oder nicht. In einer Kick-Off Veranstaltung werden die Themen für die Seminararbeiten vergeben. In den einigen wenigen Seminarsitzungen werden technische und rechtliche Grundlagen für den Einsatz von LLM-Tools gelegt. In einer Block-Veranstaltung zum Ende des Semesters werden die Erfahrungen beim Einsatz der Tools präsentiert und diskutiert.

name: Media Law and Social Media

content: The lecture is held in German. It teaches basic knowledge of media law. It is structured with interactive elements and explanations based on case studies. In the lecture, students learn legal methodology, basic structures and principles of media law, and an overview of the various sub-areas of media law using case studies. They are encouraged to identify legal peculiarities through interactive participation. The definitions of key legal terms are always taught with reference to specific case studies. In the lecture, participants also learn to independently solve specific legal questions in the context of media law by applying the definitions and legal methodology they have learned. The lecture also presents students with completely unfamiliar case studies to which they must apply the knowledge they have learned.

name: Lawful Hacking
content: Ever since modern encryption technology has existed, intelligence agencies like the NSA have been trying to find ways to break it. Due to the end-to-end encryption of many communication services today, the security authorities fear that their information channels will dry up. The security authorities are trying to counteract this by hacking into the smartphones and PCs of their citizens using the same methods as criminals. The seminar aims to comprehensively examine the phenomenon of "the state as hacker", i.e. "lawful hacking", and to answer the following key questions: Why and how does the state hack? What limits does the german Grundgesetz set? Which authorities are allowed to access citizens&#x27; devices and when, and what happens to this data afterwards? In the introductory seminar sessions, the legal foundations of Germany&#x27;s (cyber) security architecture will be laid before the students work on concrete state measures, their technical functioning and legal permissibility. Within the framework of the seminar, a guest lecture or an excursion by representatives of a security authority is planned. Representatives of the Central Office for Information Technology in the Security Sector (ZITiS) and the Bavarian Central Office for Combating Extremism and Terrorism (ZET) at the Munich Public Prosecutor&#x27;s Office have currently been requested.
title: (SOT82533) Lawful Hacking

name: Governing Innovative Technologies (BSc.) - Cloud
content:
The exponential growth of global data volume requires substantial computing power for various tasks such as data processing, storage, analytics, Machine Learning models, video streaming or gaming. Traditionally, these computing services were localized in individual companies' data centers. However, today's landscape has shifted most of these services into the 'cloud' hosted by technology giants like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.

This shift has profound sustainability implications. The cloud technology&#x27;s energy consumption, component utilization and resilience of data centers are central to ongoing discussions about sustainable computing practices. The environmental footprint of cloud technology encompasses not only energy use but also material sourcing, waste reduction and overall lifecycle management.
Moreover, the impact of cloud technology extends into various policy arenas. Policymakers have recognized the necessity to regulate and shape cloud technology, especially in regions like the European Union. Initiatives are addressing not only the strategic reliance on US-based cloud providers but also the broader sustainability challenges associated with cloud services.

To adequately comprehend the policy issues surrounding the cloud industry and its sustainability implications, students must gain a thorough understanding of the underlying technologies, business models and market dynamics. This 6-ECTS Bachelor seminar aims to provide an in-depth look into cloud computing technology, with particular emphasis on sustainability, while integrating the context of current policies and global challenges. While one building block of the seminar introduces cloud technology foundations and selected core sustainability concepts, a second one outlines key players and current themes of cloud policy in Europe and beyond. The final seminar block 

- the technology and sustainability concepts introduced in this seminar might be interesting to students from departments beyond Governance, who wish to deepen their understanding of the impact of (cloud) technology on different parts of society and policy approaches to these. Students might specifically benefit from an interdisciplinary environment in this seminar, as it mirrors the multitude of perspectives and actors involved and the requirements for collaboration across disciplines in this field.
prerequisites:
No previous experience with the technology is required or expected.

This module is for students who are.. .
1) interested in learning technical foundations for technology policy, especially related to the data economy and cloud computing technology. 
2) willing to participate in in-class discussions and engage with some (reading or video) materials before each session.
title: (SOT82840) Governing Innovative Technologies (BSc.) - Cloud X Sustainability

name: Explainable AI -- A Comprehensive Seminar on Transparent and Ethical AI
categories: Social and Political Aspects of Data Science
content:
The rapid advancement and adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across various domains have sparked concerns about the interpretability and transparency of AI systems. This MSc seminar aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of Explainable AI, focusing on techniques and best practices to make AI systems more interpretable, transparent, and accountable.

Participants will delve into a range of topics, including the importance of explainable AI, explanation techniques, interpretability in machine learning and deep learning models, post-hoc explanation methods, and their usefulness for human-AI interaction. The seminar will also address the ethical, social, and regulatory aspects of AI, exploring the role of transparency in fairness, bias mitigation, and compliance with data protection regulations.
objective:
Through presentations, paper reading, and relevant discussions on the topics, the seminar is expected to lead to the following learning results and gained competencies:

- Understanding of Explainable AI, its concepts, importance, and related challenges, along with its relationship to ethics, fairness, and accountability. 
- Understanding of different types of explanation techniques and their application and evaluation in various scenarios. 
- Knowledge about existing libraries for explainable AI and their application.  
- Scientific summary and critical discussion of research articles
prerequisites: Interest in mathematical, statistical methods, and AI in general.
title: Explainable AI -- A Comprehensive Seminar on Transparent and Ethical AI

name: Exploring Unresolved Challenges of Large Language Models
categories: Social and Political Aspects of Data Science
content:
In this seminar, we aim to address open challenges in the world of large language models (LLMs). After a more general introduction of LLMs, such as the timeline of their development, their way of working and today's state of the art, each student will dive into a specific shortcoming of these models, research it independently, and present the findings to the class. The challenges we will be focussing on can be separated into three bigger groups: 
(1) Design: problems arising before model deployment, e.g. unfathomable datasets or fine-tuning overhead.
(2) Behavior: problems arising during model deployment, e.g. outdated knowledge or misaligned behavior.
(3) Science: problems hindering academic progress, e.g. lack of experimental designs or lack of reproducibility.
Depending on the interest of the participants, we may also examine concrete applications of LLMs, as for example in the fields of law or medicine.
objective:
After successfully completing the module, the students will be able to:
(1) understand large language models, their beginnings and their development up to their current status, as well as the way they work and what they do,
(2) comprehend the capabilities of large language models and their limitations, as well as the reasons for these limitations and the solution approaches pursued so far, as well as
(3) assess the impact of these limitations on the usability of these models in different contexts.
prerequisites: Interest in AI, as well as its capabilities and limitations. Willingness to deal with (to a certain extent) technical topics.
title: (SOT86054) Exploring Unresolved Challenges of Large Language Models

name: Machine Learning and Society (6 ECTS)
categories: Social and Political Aspects of Data Science
content:
This lecture sheds light into the profound impact of machine learning (ML) on society, emphasizing the ethical, societal, and technical challenges posed by advanced algorithms. It aims to equip students with a critical understanding of the implications of ML technologies and the responsibility of practitioners in this field.
1. Algorithmic Bias
Explore the concept of bias in machine learning algorithms.
Understand how bias originates from data sources and algorithmic design.
Examine case studies where algorithmic bias has impacted decision-making in areas like recruitment, criminal justice, and lending.
2. Fairness: Formal Definitions
Introduce formal definitions of fairness in the context of machine learning.
Analyze different models of fairness and their applicability in various scenarios.
Discuss the trade-offs and challenges in implementing these models in real-world applications.
3. Alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs)
Investigate the alignment challenges in large language models.
Discuss strategies for aligning LLMs with human values and ethical norms.
Evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of these alignment strategies through practical examples.
4. Red Teaming
Learn about the practice of red teaming in the context of machine learning.
Understand how adversarial approaches can identify vulnerabilities in ML systems.
Study real-life instances where red teaming has been used to improve system robustness and safety.
5. Auditing
Examine the role of auditing in ensuring the ethical use of machine learning.
Discuss methodologies for conducting effective audits of ML systems.
Assess the impact of regulatory and compliance requirements on ML auditing processes.
6. Limits of Prediction
Investigate the theoretical and practical limits of predictive modeling in machine learning.
Understand the implications of these limits on the reliability and utility of ML predictions.
Explore scenarios where over-reliance on predictive models can lead to adverse outcomes.
7. Algorithmic Harms
Define and categorize different types of algorithmic harms.
Analyze the societal impact of these harms, with a focus on vulnerable and marginalized groups.
Discuss strategies to mitigate and prevent algorithmic harms, including policy interventions and technical solutions.
8. ML in Society
Understand how ML systems are influenced by and, in turn, influence social structures, norms, and values.
Discuss case studies that illustrate the deep interconnection between ML applications and social dynamics.
9. ML as Society
Understand the collaborative and often complex interactions between these stakeholders in the development and deployment of ML systems.
Examine the roles and responsibilities of each stakeholder group, emphasizing the ethical considerations at each stage of ML development.
Explore the concept of ML systems as socio-technical systems, where technical aspects are deeply intertwined with social, ethical, and organizational dimensions.
objective: Further information (ECTS, description of assessment methods, etc.) can be found in the module description in TUMonline.
prerequisites: Further information (ECTS, description of assessment methods, etc.) can be found in the module description in TUMonline.

name: Climate Finance
content:
The module consits of a lecture and an exercise.

Climate change is one of the critical challenges of this century. Countless studies have shown that the prosperity and health of humankind depends on the development and deployment of effective solutions to limiting global warming. Yet any such solution requires vast sums of investment. 

In 2015, the Paris Agreement underlined the responsibility of governments to align finance flows with climate change goals. Accordingly, a market for low‑carbon investments emerged, but the availability of climate finance falls short of what is needed. Thus, political discussions on the international and national levels concern how public policies can better use the financial system to accelerate climate change mitigation and adaptation. In this course, students will learn about the role of finance for the low‑carbon transition in developing as well as industrialized countries. We will discuss existing policies, their effectiveness and the underlying political economy challenges to implementing them. Combining recent academic findings, policy papers and hands‑on insights from the lecturers and guests, we will analyze structural challenges, conflicting positions in international negotiations and domestic policy‑making, and the role of multilateral financial institutions. As such, the module links directly to ongoing internaitonal negotiations on climate finance.

The module is structured into four thematic parts: 1) Introduction to climate finance (input); 2) Financial flows and instruments for the climate (presentations); 3) International climate finance flows (presentations); 4) Policy-making in the UNFCCC process (input and term paper).

name: Algorithms & Fundamental Rights
categories: Social and Political Aspects of Data Science
content:
Introduction to Algorithms and Fundamental Rights:
This section introduces the basic concepts of algorithms and fundamental rights, focusing on how algorithmic decisions can impact societal norms.
Algorithmic Decision-Making:
An exploration of how algorithms are used in decision-making processes, including examples from various sectors such as criminal justice, employment, and social services.
Philosophical Foundations of Fundamental Rights I - Autonomy and Algorithms:
This session delves into the concept of autonomy and its relationship with algorithms. It explores how algorithmic systems can support or undermine individual autonomy, highlighting ethical considerations and philosophical debates.
Philosophical Foundations of Fundamental Rights II - Rule of Law:
This session emphasizes the principle of the rule of law in the context of algorithmic systems. It examines how algorithms can be aligned with or deviate from the rule of law, discussing the implications for justice and governance.
Accountability:
This section deals with the principles of transparency and accountability in algorithmic systems. It explores methods for ensuring transparency and accountability in practice.
Case Studies in Algorithmic Impact:
Detailed case studies illustrating the real-world impact of algorithms on fundamental rights, fostering critical analysis and discussion among students.
Future Directions and Solutions:
The module concludes with a discussion of emerging trends and potential solutions to address the challenges posed by algorithmic systems to fundamental rights, with an emphasis on strategies to uphold standards and societal values.

prerequisites: An interest in the intersection of technology, law, and human rights, as well as a willingness to engage with interdisciplinary content are assumed. No prior knowledge of legal or philosophical concepts is required, as these will be covered during the course.
